title: Smoke inhalation
why_this_matters: Smoke causes hypoxia and airway injury, and oxygen must not wait for a reassuring pulse oximeter reading, which can be falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning [1].

what_changes_from_human.point: Give oxygen immediately in suspected smoke inhalation. A normal oxygen saturation can be falsely elevated in carbon monoxide poisoning [1].
Human practice around cyanide antidotes and hyperbaric oxygen is human evidence; nothing canine was retrieved for either [5][6].

recognition: Smoke contains harmful gases, chemicals and superheated particles. It causes generalized hypoxia and airway inflammation from impaired oxygen transport and use, plus thermal and chemical airway injury [1].

In 9 dogs and 13 cats presented within 12 hours of house fires: sooting, coughing and polypnea; tachycardia, polypnea, hypothermia and pink mucous membranes; hemoconcentration, mixed acid-base disorders and moderate carboxyhemoglobinemia [2].
management: Immediate oxygen therapy is mandatory for all suspected smoke inhalation patients and should not be delayed for diagnostics or a normal saturation reading [1].
Treatment is generally supportive: oxygen and airway management, including chest physiotherapy, bronchodilators and nebulization [1].
Patients with mild signs who respond to initial stabilization generally have a favorable prognosis. Severe signs, or progression despite stabilization, may need advanced or intensive care [1].
In the small-animal series, one cat died and 21 animals were discharged within 0 to 6 days. Outcome is good when animals are treated early with oxygen and fluids [2].

takeaway: Start oxygen at once, do not be reassured by a normal saturation, and expect airway swelling to progress.
